passage: Last month Nitin trapped me by the water cooler. He kept grabbing my lunch box and laughing, and his friends blocked the way out. My heart was banging so hard I could hear it, and my face went hot. Then I shoved him hard. Later I sat in the office feeling sick with shame. I kept thinking, I'm not a pusher. I'm Dilnaz, the quiet one. Ms Rao, the counsellor, didn't shout. She asked what my body did first. I told her about my heart and hot face. "That's your body getting ready to fight," she said. "It doesn't make you a bad person." She said she would speak to Nitin's class teacher too. We practised what to do next time: step back and call a teacher.

qa.q: Where did Nitin trap Dilnaz?
qa.a: Nitin trapped Dilnaz by the water cooler.

qa.q: How did Dilnaz feel sitting in the office afterwards?
qa.a: Dilnaz felt sick with shame and confused, thinking "I'm not a pusher".

qa.q: How did Ms Rao's question about the body help Dilnaz?
qa.a: By asking what Dilnaz's body did first, Ms Rao helped Dilnaz see the shove as a fight reaction to being trapped, and they planned a safer step for next time.

qa.q: How might Ms Rao see the shove differently from how Dilnaz first saw it?
qa.a: Ms Rao sees it as a body reacting to being cornered, while Dilnaz first took it as proof of being a bad person.

grounding: A cornered child lashes out, then feels ashamed, and understands it better once the pounding heart and hot face are named.

passage:
Note for Varun's file, Class 5B. Leela Menon, class teacher.
Today after lunch, two classmates stood over Varun's desk, calling him names and tearing his drawing. Before I reached them, Varun bolted out of the room. I found him on the back stairs, breathing fast, face red, fists pressed to his knees. He said, "I ran away like a baby." I sat two steps below him and waited. Then I said, "Your heart was racing and your face was hot. Your body told you to get away. That's not babyish." He nodded slowly, and his breathing eased. I have spoken to the two classmates and will inform their parents. I will phone Varun's mother this evening, and he will sit near my desk this week.

qa.q: Where did Leela find Varun?
qa.a: Leela found Varun on the back stairs.

qa.q: What was Varun feeling when he said he "ran away like a baby"?
qa.a: Varun felt ashamed of running and was judging himself harshly for it.

qa.q: What did Leela do that helped Varun understand rather than judge himself?
qa.a: Leela sat nearby and waited, then named his racing heart and hot face as his body telling him to get away.

qa.q: What would change if Leela had first scolded Varun for leaving the room?
qa.a: Varun would likely feel more ashamed and scared, and might bolt again instead of calming and trusting Leela.

grounding: A cornered child bolts from class and feels ashamed, and an adult names the body's signals so he can understand instead of judging himself.

'Farida, sit. You're not in trouble here. Can you tell me what happened by the lockers?'
'Those girls took my bag again and backed me into the corner. Then I pushed Sana really hard and ran out.' Farida stared at her shoes. 'I'm horrible. I never push anyone.'
'What was your body doing just before you pushed?'
'My heart was banging. My face went hot. My hands just... did it.'
'That's your body trying to protect you when you feel trapped. It happens fast, before thinking. It doesn't make you horrible.'
'But I hurt her.'
'We'll talk about making that right. And those girls cornering you is not okay either. I'm going to speak to your class teacher about them today, and we'll ring your Ammi together before you go home.'
Farida nodded. 'Okay, Miss Jyoti.'

qa.q: What did Farida do right after pushing Sana?
qa.a: Ran out.

qa.q: What was Farida feeling as she stared at her shoes?
qa.a: Farida felt ashamed and guilty, saying 'I'm horrible' because Farida never pushes anyone.

qa.q: How did Miss Jyoti help Farida understand what happened?
qa.a: She helped Farida name the pounding heart and hot face, explained it as the body's way of protecting against feeling trapped, and acted on the bullying the same day while still planning to make things right with Sana.

qa.q: What would change if Miss Jyoti had only punished Farida for pushing?
qa.a: Farida would feel even more ashamed, the girls doing the cornering would carry on, and Farida would not understand what happened in the body.

grounding: Shows a cornered child lashing out and fleeing, then feeling ashamed, and an adult who helps the child name the body signals rather than self-judge.

passage: I still remember my legs deciding before I did. It was Class 5, and Arnab had me backed against the stair railing, holding my tiffin over the drop and laughing with his friends. My heart was going like a drum and my face was burning. Then I ran, past the class teacher's desk and into the washroom, and stayed till the bell. I felt like the biggest coward in school. Mr Kurian, the sports teacher, found me there. He didn't tell me off. He asked, 'Pranav, what was your body doing just then?' I told him about the drum and the heat. 'That's your body getting you away from danger. Running isn't cowardly.' Then he took me straight to my class teacher, who called Arnab in that afternoon and phoned my parents before home time. I still get the drum sometimes. Now I know its name.

qa.q: Where did Pranav run and hide?
qa.a: Into the washroom, where Pranav stayed till the bell.

qa.q: What was Pranav feeling after running away?
qa.a: Pranav felt ashamed and cowardly, as if running had been a weakness rather than a reaction.

qa.q: Which step by Mr Kurian mattered most, and why?
qa.a: Asking what Pranav's body was doing helped turn shame into understanding, and taking the matter to the class teacher the same afternoon dealt with the bullying.

qa.q: How might Arnab's friends have seen the moment Pranav ran?
qa.a: They may have treated it as funny or a win, without noticing how frightened Pranav was.

grounding: Shows a child who bolts when cornered by a bully and feels ashamed, and how naming the pounding heart and hot face helps the child understand rather than judge the reaction.

passage:
Playground duty note, Thursday
At lunch an older boy cornered Wasim against the back fence and grabbed his cricket cap. Wasim swung and hit him on the arm, then ran and hid behind the water tank. I checked the older boy was unhurt and sent him to the office with another teacher, then went to Wasim. He was crouched, fists tight, breathing fast. 'I'm bad,' he said. I sat on the ground a little distance away and asked what his body was doing. 'My heart's too fast and my face is on fire.' I told him that is what a body does when it feels trapped, and that we would sort out the hitting calmly later. The head teacher came out at once, spoke to the older boy and phoned both families before home time. Wasim's father has been told; Wasim will meet the counsellor tomorrow.
Rashmi, lunch supervisor

qa.q: Where did Wasim hide after hitting the older boy?
qa.a: Behind the water tank.

qa.q: What was Wasim feeling when he said 'I'm bad'?
qa.a: He felt ashamed of hitting, and still frightened, with his heart too fast and his face on fire.

qa.q: What did Rashmi do in the right order?
qa.a: Rashmi made sure both boys were safe, then sat calmly near Wasim, helped him name his body signals and left the talk about the hitting for later.

qa.q: How might the older boy's actions look different once the head teacher hears the whole story?
qa.a: The head teacher can see that the older boy cornered Wasim first, so the hitting is understood as a fight reaction to being trapped, and the cornering is dealt with too.

grounding: Shows a cornered child lashing out and fleeing, then calling himself bad, and an adult helping him name his racing heart and hot face instead of judging himself.

passage:
Thursday
Today Hemant and his gang cornered me behind the water tank again and grabbed my tiffin. My heart was banging so hard I could hear it, and my face went burning hot. I shoved Hemant really hard and he fell, and then I just ran, out of the gate, all the way to the bus stop. I feel so ashamed. I'm not a pushing person.
But Ms Rao found me at the bus stop. She didn't shout. She sat with me and asked what my body felt. I told her: banging heart, hot face, legs wanting to run. She said that's the body's alarm, not me being bad. She phoned Mummy this evening and is meeting Hemant's parents tomorrow. Mummy hugged me for ages.
Arohi

qa.q: Where did Hemant's gang corner Arohi?
qa.a: Behind the water tank.

qa.q: How does Arohi feel about pushing Hemant?
qa.a: Arohi feels ashamed and upset, writing 'I'm not a pushing person.'

qa.q: How did Ms Rao help Arohi understand what happened?
qa.a: She calmly asked what Arohi's body felt, explained the banging heart and hot face were the body's alarm, phoned Mummy and planned to meet Hemant's parents.

qa.q: How might Mummy have felt after Ms Rao's call?
qa.a: Mummy probably felt worried and protective, hugging Arohi for ages.

grounding: A child cornered by a bully lashes out and bolts, feels ashamed, and an adult helps name the body's alarm.
